clinicalPearls: SPG32 is a rare autosomal recessive, complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia mapped to chromosome 14q12-q21, with no confirmed causative gene.
It was delineated in a consanguineous Portuguese family and combines spastic paraparesis with mild intellectual (cognitive) impairment.
Onset is typically in childhood, with slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity and learning or developmental difficulties.
Characteristic neuroimaging features include a thin corpus callosum together with cerebellar and cerebral cortical atrophy.
Pontine dysraphia (a midline pontine cleft) has been described as a distinctive radiological marker of this subtype.
The imaging overlap with SPG11 and SPG15 (thin corpus callosum HSP) is important, and these testable genes should be excluded.
No clinical genetic test exists for the SPG32 locus, so diagnosis is clinical, radiological and by exclusion.
Management is symptomatic and supportive — spasticity treatment, physiotherapy and educational or cognitive support.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG32 is an autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia localised by linkage to chromosome 14q12-q21 in a consanguineous Portuguese family; no gene within the region has been confirmed and the molecular pathway remains undefined. The progressive spastic paraparesis follows the general HSP mechanism of length-dependent corticospinal tract degeneration, while the accompanying mild intellectual impairment and the structural findings of a thin corpus callosum, cerebellar and cortical atrophy and pontine dysraphia point to a gene product important for central nervous system development and axonal or commissural integrity. This developmental, thin-corpus-callosum phenotype places SPG32 among the complicated recessive HSPs alongside SPG11 and SPG15, from which it is distinguished chiefly by its distinct chromosomal locus and the associated pontine cleft.
additionalDifferentials: SPG11 (spatacsin) — recessive HSP with thin corpus callosum and cognitive decline, the closest mimic
SPG15 (spastizin/ZFYVE26) — recessive HSP with thin corpus callosum, Kjellin syndrome
SPG21 (maspardin) — Mast syndrome, recessive complicated HSP with cognitive and psychiatric features
SPG35 (FA2H) and other complicated recessive HSPs with white matter change
Cerebral palsy (non-progressive) and other causes of thin corpus callosum with spasticity
Congenital disorders of glycosylation and metabolic leukoencephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain to demonstrate thin corpus callosum, cortical and cerebellar atrophy and pontine dysraphia
Genetic testing of testable thin-corpus-callosum HSP genes (SPG11, SPG15 and others) and exome analysis
Neuropsychological and cognitive assessment to characterise the intellectual impairment
MRI spine to exclude structural myelopathy
Nerve conduction studies to assess for associated neuropathy
Metabolic screen to exclude leukoencephalopathies and congenital disorders of glycosylation
redFlags: Regression or loss of previously acquired skills suggesting a progressive metabolic leukoencephalopathy rather than a slowly progressive HSP
Seizures or rapidly progressive cognitive decline needing urgent evaluation
Rapid motor deterioration atypical for the slow HSP course
Focal neurological deficits or features of raised intracranial pressure suggesting a structural lesion
reference.prognosis: SPG32 is slowly progressive with childhood onset. The combination of spastic paraparesis and mild intellectual impairment leads to gradually increasing mobility and learning needs, but life expectancy is generally preserved.
pitfalls: Labelling childhood spasticity with cognitive impairment as cerebral palsy and missing a progressive inherited disorder
Assuming a thin corpus callosum HSP must be SPG11 or SPG15 and not recognising the distinct SPG32 locus
Expecting a confirmatory gene test, which does not exist for this locus
Missing the pontine dysraphia and other imaging clues by not reviewing dedicated midline sagittal sequences
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical genetics reviews
Neurogenetics reference databases (gene and locus catalogues)
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; treat lower-limb spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and walking aids to maintain gait and prevent contractures
Educational and neuropsychological support for the associated mild intellectual impairment
Monitor developmental progress and mobility with periodic rehabilitation input
Consider intrathecal baclofen for spasticity refractory to oral and focal treatment
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with carrier testing and consanguinity-related recurrence-risk discussion
Escalate to multidisciplinary neurology and rehabilitation as disability accrues
